title: Debugging and Development Tools: Finding and Fixing Bugs Like a Professional

questions.question: A program averages numbers using `total * count` instead of `total / count`. It runs fine but prints wrong results. This is a:
options: Syntax error
Runtime error
Logic error
Compile-time error
questions.rationale: Logic errors never crash — the program runs and produces a wrong answer, which is why only tests and careful reading catch them.

questions.question: In the professional debugging loop, what should you do FIRST?
options: Rewrite the module from scratch
Change random lines until it works
Reproduce the bug on demand
Deploy to production and watch
questions.rationale: The loop is reproduce → isolate → hypothesize → test → fix → regression-test; without reliable reproduction you can never know the fix worked.

questions.question: Bisecting a bug means:
options: Trying every possibility in order
Cutting the remaining suspicious range roughly in half each time, so a million possibilities need about twenty probes
Deleting half the source files
Splitting the bug report among teammates
questions.rationale: Bisecting halves the remaining search space each step — git bisect applies exactly this idea to commits.

questions.question: When reading a stack trace, which frame should you examine first?
options: The bottom frame, which is always main()
It does not matter
The longest frame
The top frame — it is where the error actually happened
questions.rationale: The top frame names where the error occurred; the frames below it are the callers in reverse order — the path from the crime scene back to the door.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'step over' and 'step into' in a debugger?
options: Step over executes the next line without entering functions it calls; step into dives inside the next function call
Step over skips the next line entirely without running it; step into runs it
Step into only works on breakpoints; step over works on watchpoints
They are identical in every debugger
questions.rationale: Step over runs the next line at the current level, treating function calls as single steps; step into descends into the called function to watch inside it.

questions.question: Why is logging preferred over scattered print statements?
options: Logs are always faster than print
Print statements cannot display numbers
Logging is permanent, level-tagged, and filterable by severity without editing code
Logs remove the need for tests
questions.rationale: Logs carry levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) that can be filtered without touching code, and they need not be stripped out like temporary prints.

questions.question: In Git, what does a merge conflict usually mean?
options: The repository is corrupted
Two branches edited the same lines, so Git asks you to choose the resolution
You forgot to run git clone
The commit message was invalid
questions.rationale: A conflict arises only when two branches change the same lines; Git pauses the merge and asks you to pick the correct combined result.

questions.question: In the testing pyramid, why do unit tests form the broad base?
options: They run in milliseconds and can number in the thousands, using mocks to isolate one function or class
They exercise the whole system through the real UI
They are required by law
They replace the need for integration tests
questions.rationale: Unit tests are the many, fast, isolated tests of the pyramid; mocks replace collaborators like databases, while end-to-end tests are few, slow, and closest to the user.

questions.question: The three beats of test-driven development are:
options: Plan, code, ship
Red — write a failing test; green — make it pass minimally; refactor — clean up while staying green
Write code, write tests, delete code
Commit, push, pull
questions.rationale: TDD's rhythm is red-green-refactor: the failing test describes the desired behavior, minimal code makes it pass, and refactoring cleans both while the suite stays green.

questions.question: According to the lesson's timebox guidance, how long should you struggle alone before asking for help?
options: Never ask for help under any circumstances
A bounded slot of roughly 30–45 minutes, then seek help
At least one full week
Ask immediately without trying anything
questions.rationale: Struggle deliberately for a bounded 30–45 minute slot — enough to learn from the problem — then ask well: goal, expected vs actual, what you tried, versions, and a minimal example.
